title: Signal No. 2 on a Sunday
note: Fictional unit and patients. Your unit protocol, the attending nephrologist and your local disaster authorities decide every real event.
intro: PAGASA has raised Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 for Bulacan. You are the head nurse of a 16-station unit in Malolos, also acting as safety nurse. The plan says: “Signal No. 2: activate the call-down; ask the attending nephrologist about early dialysis.” The Monday–Wednesday–Friday group has 30 patients.

choices.text: You are the on-call lead: activate it now, log the time, and tell the managers.
choices.feedback: The plan names who activates it. Logging the time starts the record and the clock. Tell the unit manager and the Dialysis Clinical Head.

choices.text: Wait until Monday morning to see how the storm develops before activating anything.
choices.feedback: Signal No. 2 means gale-force winds within 24 hours. Monday morning is too late to move sessions or reach staff.
choices.then: At 2:00 p.m. the unit manager calls and asks why nothing has started. You activate.

choices.text: Text each staff member to decide for themselves what to do, since they know their own roads best.
choices.feedback: A plan with no lead is not a plan. One person activates; everyone else follows the plan.
choices.then: Replies conflict, so you activate the plan formally.

n2.prompt: In what order do you call?

choices.text: Staff first, then the 30 Monday patients, then the rest.
choices.feedback: Capacity is set by staff. Patients get a real answer only once you know who can come. Staff first to know who can work Monday, especially the charge nurse from the flood-prone barangay.

choices.text: Monday patients first, since they are the ones at risk, and then staff once the patients are informed.
choices.feedback: Patients hear early, but you may promise sessions you cannot staff.
choices.then: Two patients are told to come early before you know the shift can run; you call them back.

choices.text: Post the whole call list, with addresses, in the staff and patient group chat so everyone can help call.
choices.feedback: The call list is personal data under the Data Privacy Act. Share it only with the callers.
choices.then: The records officer removes the post and you split the list among three callers.

n3.scene: Twelve staff can work Monday. Five Monday patients live in barangays that flooded last year; two had potassium above 6 mmol/L last week.
n3.prompt: What do you do about early dialysis?

choices.text: Call the attending nephrologist with the flagged Monday list and ask who comes early.
choices.feedback: Early dialysis is the nephrologist’s decision. Your job is to give the facts and then make the roster work. Flags: flood-prone barangays, recent high potassium, large weight gains; ask for a decision on who comes early and when.

choices.text: Move all 30 patients to a shortened Sunday night session yourself, without calling the nephrologist.
choices.feedback: Any change to schedule or session length is the nephrologist’s decision, and shortened sessions need a written order and the six conditions.
choices.then: The nephrologist hears of it, stops the plan, and decides on 9 patients for early dialysis.

choices.text: Do nothing about early dialysis until Signal No. 3 is raised, since the track may still change.
choices.feedback: Signal No. 3 brings storm-force winds within 18 hours; roads may already be closing.
choices.then: At 3:00 p.m. you call the nephrologist after all.

n4.scene: Calling the receiving unit in the plan, you learn its contact person retired in June.

choices.text: Call the unit’s main line for the current contact, add a second receiving unit, record both fixes.
choices.feedback: A receiving unit is useful only if someone there answers and expects your patients. Confirm capacity, and write both fixes into the after-action notes.

choices.text: Assume the unit will still take patients if needed, since the agreement is signed and still valid.
choices.feedback: Without a named contact, a patient may arrive at a unit that cannot take them.
choices.then: Monday, a patient is turned away and you find the new contact then.

end.title: Sunday night
end.text: Nine patients dialyze early on Sunday evening, staff know Monday’s plan, and two receiving units are confirmed. The after-action notes list three fixes: deputies for every role, receiving-unit contacts checked yearly, and a call-down drill before the season.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • One named person activates the plan, and logs the time.
  • Staff first, then patients due soonest. Protect the call list as personal data.
  • Early dialysis is the nephrologist’s decision; the unit supplies the facts and the roster.
